TP63 is a p53-family sequence-specific transcription factor that acts as a transcriptional activator at its target promoters and enhancers. In this context the regulatory edge is annotated as TP63 → HNRNPL, meaning TP63 provides positive input to HNRNPL expression. The causal chain runs: TP63 loss-of-function (CRISPR knockout/knockdown) → loss of TP63 protein occupancy at its response elements in the HNRNPL promoter/enhancer → reduced recruitment of coactivators and RNA polymerase II and less productive transcription initiation → decreased HNRNPL mRNA, and consequently decreased hnRNPL protein. Because the perturbation removes an activating regulator rather than a repressor, the target moves in the same direction as the regulator — down. The effect is expected in the matched control context, so the comparison is against unperturbed cells of the same cell type and condition, where TP63 is intact and continues to drive basal HNRNPL transcription. Only if TP63 were acting as a repressor at this locus (or if a compensatory paralog such as TP53/TP73 or another hnRNP compensated) would the direction reverse; under the standard annotation of an activating regulatory edge, the expected direction is down.

TET2 is the 5-methylcytosine dioxygenase that keeps CpG dinucleotides at active enhancers and at the regulatory elements of ESR1 in an unmethylated, 5hmC-marked state; its loss (as in Tet2 knockout/haploinsufficiency) causes the ESR1 promoter and enhancer regions to become hypermethylated, so ESR1/ERα is transcriptionally silenced — a reduction seen already at the heterozygous dose and accompanied by global 5mC gain. TET2 loss additionally strips ERα of its coactivator function, since TET2 occupies the same active enhancers as ERα and its depletion impairs E2-dependent ERα recruitment to those elements, so both the amount of ESR1 and the DNA-binding activity of the remaining ERα fall. Because PTGES is an ESR1/ERα target whose transcription depends on ERα occupancy at its regulatory elements, cutting the upstream ERα input lowers PTGES transcription. The order is therefore: TET2 loss → loss of 5hmC and hypermethylation of ESR1 regulatory DNA → decreased ESR1 expression plus weakened ERα enhancer binding → reduced ERα-driven transactivation of PTGES → PTGES expression down relative to the matched unperturbed control.

Rragd is a positively regulated (activated) GATA1 target whose +4 kb regulatory element carries a single GATA motif that GATA1 can only occupy with FOG1/ZFPM1 acting as a chromatin-occupancy facilitator. The D218G substitution sits in the GATA1 N-terminal zinc finger and does not impair DNA binding, but it weakens the GATA1–FOG1 protein–protein interaction; the order of events is therefore: weakened GATA1–FOG1 binding → loss/instability of GATA1 occupancy at the FOG1-dependent Rragd +4 kb element and failure to assemble the activating complex there (FOG1, plus associated coactivators and the GATA1/TAL1–LMO2–LDB1 machinery at erythroid loci) → reduced RNA Pol II loading and lower Rragd transcription. In G1E/G1ME complementation assays, N-finger mutants that disrupt FOG1 binding reduce GATA1-dependent gene activation, and D218G does so in the same direction as wild-type GATA1 but more weakly — this is the mildest FOG1-binding allele, so the reduction in Rragd is expected to be modest in magnitude while still downward. Note the direction holds because the element is an activating, FOG1-dependent site; FOG1-independent GATA1 repression targets would move the opposite way, and here activation is impaired more than repression for D218G.

H2A.Z (H2AFZ)-containing nucleosomes flank the nucleosome-depleted regions of active promoters and enhancers and are required for their accessibility and function. Because ZHX2 is a TP63 target, its regulation is expected to run through a TP63-bound promoter/enhancer element, and H2A.Z turnover at that element is what keeps it accessible and competent for transcription-factor engagement. When H2A.Z is lost or reduced, the ordered chain is: reduced H2A.Z deposition/turnover → impaired nucleosome eviction and chromatin accessibility at the ZHX2 regulatory element → weakened TP63 occupancy and loss of TP63-dependent activation → decreased RNA Pol II recruitment/initiation at the ZHX2 promoter → lower ZHX2 mRNA. In other words, H2A.Z acts upstream as a permissive chromatin cofactor for the TP63→ZHX2 regulatory axis, so removing it is expected to decrease, not increase, ZHX2 expression relative to the matched unperturbed control.

Perturbation acts directly on the perturbed entity (KCNK5 expression), so the primary, most proximal effect is on KCNK5's own transcript: a loss-or-reduction intervention (CRISPRi/RNAi-style knockdown of the gene or its promoter) lowers KCNK5 mRNA relative to the matched unperturbed control in the same context. No intermediate mediator is required for this step — the causal order is simply perturbation → reduced KCNK5 transcription/transcript level. ESR1 sits upstream as the regulator of KCNK5, but it is not itself the perturbed node here, so its activation status is unchanged and cannot offset the direct loss: if ESR1-dependent activation of the KCNK5 promoter is what maintains baseline expression, removing that output (by knocking down KCNK5) yields a net decrease, not a compensatory increase. The one assumption worth flagging is that the intervention targets KCNK5 itself rather than ESR1 activity; under that reading the expected direction is up, since an activating regulator's loss would de-repress/down-regulate its target. Given the stated perturbed entity, the answer is down.

ESR1 encodes ERα, a ligand-dependent nuclear receptor that binds estrogen-response elements in the TFF1 promoter/enhancer and, together with coactivators (e.g. NCOA/SRC family, p300/CBP), recruits RNA polymerase II to drive TFF1 transcription. TFF1 is therefore a canonical positively regulated ERα target, so loss or reduction of the upstream regulator removes that activation and TFF1 transcript levels fall relative to the matched control — the order being ESR1 loss → loss of ERE occupancy and coactivator recruitment → reduced Pol II initiation at the TFF1 promoter → lower TFF1 mRNA. The same downward direction holds if the perturbation instead removes TFF1 transcript directly, since either way the activated ESR1→TFF1 arm is broken before TFF1 output is measured.

Pdk4 is a canonical, direct PPARα target (activated as a PPARα–RXRα heterodimer on its regulatory regions), so the question reduces to what BHLHE40 does to PPARα's transcriptional output. BHLHE40 is not a repressor of this program: in hepatocytes it occupies the same enhancer clusters as PPARα/RXRα/HNF4α, and its proximal-proteome includes RXRα plus PPARα coactivators and corepressors — it behaves as a required cofactor/co-activator for PPARα-driven gene activation. Loss of BHLHE40 therefore leaves the PPARα–RXRα complex without this cofactor, weakening recruitment/activation and lowering transcription of PPARα targets. Consistent with this order — BHLHE40 loss → reduced PPARα–RXRα transactivation → less Pdk4 mRNA — *Bhlhe40* knockdown in primary hepatocytes blunts the induction of Pdk4 along with Hmgcs2 and Angptl4. Expected direction relative to the matched control: Pdk4 goes **down**.

ZNF143 acts as a sequence-specific transcriptional activator that binds the SPH/SPH-like motif in promoter regions and recruits coactivators to load RNA polymerase II and drive transcription. Because ARID5A sits downstream of ZNF143 as its direct target, loss or reduction of ZNF143 removes that activating input at the ARID5A promoter, so the ARID5A locus is transcribed less and ARID5A mRNA (and subsequently protein) declines relative to the matched unperturbed control — direction of effect propagates ZNF143 → ARID5A promoter occupancy → transcriptional output, with the decrease in ARID5A manifesting after the primary loss of the ZNF143 activator.

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific C2H2 zinc-finger transcriptional activator that binds SBS/SPH motifs in promoters (often together with CTCF/cohesin at promoter anchors of chromatin loops), so a ZNF143-binding site in the CCPG1 promoter is a positive, cis-acting input to that gene. Depleting ZNF143 removes that occupancy — the promoter loses its activating factor and, where loop architecture is involved, the contacts that bring enhancer-bound coactivators into proximity of the CCPG1 promoter. Order of events: ZNF143 loss → reduced promoter binding → less recruitment of coactivators/RNA Pol II initiation → decreased CCPG1 transcription → lower steady-state CCPG1 mRNA (and protein) relative to the unperturbed control. Caveat: the direction is inverted if ZNF143 acts as a repressor at this locus or if CCPG1 is under compensatory feedback, but given the stated activating regulatory relationship, the expected direction is down.

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific promoter-binding protein that acts predominantly as a transcriptional activator, so the direction here tracks the loss of a positive regulator. Order of events: knocking down or depleting ZNF143 removes it from its cognate motif in the CREBL2 promoter/enhancer region → the activating signal at that element (recruitment of co-activators and RNA Pol II, plus ZNF143's role in maintaining promoter–enhancer looping) is lost → the CREBL2 locus shifts toward a less permissive chromatin/transcription state → CREBL2 mRNA and protein fall relative to the matched unperturbed control. The key mediator is therefore the promoter-bound ZNF143 activator complex itself, not a downstream signaling cascade; the drop is a direct, proximal consequence of losing the transcription factor. Note that this holds because the annotation specifies ZNF143 as the regulator of CREBL2 — if the regulation were repressive in the particular cell context, the sign would invert, which is why the activation direction should be confirmed from the source annotation.

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific transcriptional activator that binds its cognate promoter/enhancer motif and recruits coactivators and the general transcription machinery; ERAL1 is a direct ZNF143 target. The causal order is: loss/reduction of ZNF143 → decreased ZNF143 occupancy at the ERAL1 regulatory region → weakened promoter activation and coactivator recruitment → reduced ERAL1 transcription and steady-state mRNA. So relative to the matched unperturbed control in the same context, ERAL1 expression is expected to go down. This holds specifically because the ZNF143–ERAL1 edge is activating; had ZNF143 been a repressor at that locus, the sign would flip.

Under loss-or-reduction of ZNF143, the GTPBP8 locus loses that activating input, so the order runs: reduced ZNF143 protein → decreased occupancy at the GTPBP8 regulatory element → weaker Pol II recruitment/initiation → lower GTPBP8 mRNA, and consequently less GTPBP8 protein. Because the perturbation removes a positive regulator rather than a repressor or a compensatory feedback arm, the matched unperturbed control in the same context would sit at the higher basal level, and the perturbed sample is expected to move downward.

ZNF143 is a zinc-finger transcription factor that binds the STAF/SBS motif at promoters and acts as a positive regulator — it recruits RNA Pol II and helps organize enhancer–promoter looping at its target loci. JUND (an AP-1 family immediate-early gene) has ZNF143 occupied at its promoter region, so reducing ZNF143 lowers its occupancy there, which weakens promoter activation and looping-dependent transcription and therefore reduces JUND mRNA output. The order is: ZNF143 loss → decreased ZNF143 binding at the JUND promoter (and its associated chromatin contacts) → reduced transcriptional initiation/elongation by Pol II → lower steady-state JUND expression relative to the matched unperturbed control. (Because JUND is also driven by MAPK/AP-1–responsive signaling, the readout should be measured on a comparable signaling background, but the ZNF143-dependent component moves in the down direction.)

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific transcriptional activator (a C2H2 zinc-finger protein that recognizes the SBS/CTCCC-type motif and acts as a general "housekeeping" activator, also implicated in chromatin looping between promoters and enhancers). Because the perturbation reduces ZNF143 levels, the transcription factor is no longer present at the MFSD3 promoter/enhancer to recruit coactivators such as p300/CBP and the Mediator complex, so the productive RNA Pol II initiation/elongation machinery is not assembled as efficiently. The causal order is: ZNF143 loss → reduced ZNF143 occupancy at MFSD3 regulatory elements → loss of coactivator recruitment and lower transcriptional initiation → decreased MFSD3 mRNA. The net expectation is therefore a decrease, not an increase; note that this assumes ZNF143 acts as the direct activator in this context rather than as a repressor or indirect modifier, which would need ChIP/qPCR or RNA-seq confirmation.

PAPOLG sits downstream of ZNF143 in this regulatory chain, so the causal order is: ZNF143 protein depletion → loss of ZNF143 occupancy at the PAPOLG promoter → reduced coactivator recruitment and lower Pol II initiation → decreased PAPOLG transcription and a consequent drop in steady-state PAPOLG mRNA. Nothing in this axis is inhibitory or compensatory-activating, so removing the activator shifts PAPOLG expression downward relative to the matched unperturbed control.

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific DNA-binding activator that occupies SBS (ZNF143-binding site) motifs in the proximal promoters/TSS of its target genes and drives transcription, so PROSER3 expression depends on ZNF143 being present to transactivate its promoter. Reducing ZNF143 therefore removes a positive input: ZNF143 occupancy at the PROSER3 promoter falls, promoter activity and RNA Pol II loading at that locus decrease, and nascent PROSER3 transcription drops — the mediator is the loss of ZNF143-dependent promoter activation, and the order is ZNF143 depletion → reduced promoter binding/activation → lower PROSER3 mRNA. Because the question asks for the expectation relative to the matched unperturbed control in the same context, the direction is downward; the magnitude would depend on how much residual ZNF143 remains and on any compensatory factors.

ZNF143 acts as a transcriptional activator, so RNF40 is read out as a positively regulated direct target rather than a repressed one (the mechanism field here is empty, so this rests on ZNF143's general activator role rather than a stated repression mode). Order of events: reducing ZNF143 first lowers occupancy of its SBS motif at the RNF40 promoter/enhancer; because ZNF143 typically works by recruiting co-activators and supporting promoter–enhancer looping rather than by repressing, the loss of that occupancy removes activating input; the RNF40 locus consequently loses transcriptional drive, giving lower steady-state RNF40 mRNA than the matched unperturbed control in the same cellular context. The key mediator is therefore ZNF143 itself as the limiting activator of the RNF40 locus — a depletion-and-readout logic, not a signaling cascade — with the direction of change (down) following directly from the activator sign and the loss-or-reduction intervention.

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific transcriptional activator that binds the SBS (SPH/ZnF143) motif in promoters and enhancers and drives transcription, frequently as part of chromatin-organizing complexes such as SMC5/6. Since SNRNP70 is a ZNF143 target, its regulatory element carries a ZNF143 binding site, so ZNF143 acts as a positive input rather than a repressor. When ZNF143 is lost or reduced, the causal chain runs in this order: ZNF143 protein depletion → loss of ZNF143 occupancy at the SNRNP70 cis-regulatory element → reduced enhancer activation and promoter RNA Pol II recruitment, with weakened enhancer–promoter looping → decreased transcription initiation at the SNRNP70 promoter → lower SNRNP70 mRNA (and consequently less U1-70K protein). The key mediator is ZNF143 itself as the direct DNA-bound activator; no compensatory repressor is needed, because the effect is simply withdrawal of a positive regulator. Relative to the matched unperturbed control, SNRNP70 expression is therefore expected to go down.

ZNF143 (also known as SBF/STAF) is a zinc-finger, sequence-specific transcriptional **activator** that binds CCAAT-like motifs at promoters and enhancers, where it recruits coactivators and supports RNA polymerase II loading. So in this loss-or-reduction experiment, the causal chain runs: ZNF143 knockdown → loss of activator occupancy at the THOP1 regulatory region → reduced initiation of THOP1 transcription → lower steady-state THOP1 mRNA. If the readout is protein rather than transcript, the fall comes one step later still, via reduced translation of the smaller mRNA pool. The direction is therefore a decrease relative to the matched unperturbed control; a rise would only be expected if ZNF143 were acting as a repressor or if the locus were under compensatory relief from another factor, neither of which is implied here.

ZNF143 is a C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factor that acts as a sequence-specific activator: it binds the SPH/GTGCCAGC-type motif at promoters and enhancers and, in addition to recruiting RNA Pol II and coactivators, it helps establish promoter–enhancer looping through its role in chromatin architecture. Because it is a positive regulator of UBALD1 — it occupies the UBALD1 regulatory region and drives its transcription — reducing ZNF143 levels lowers promoter occupancy, weakens enhancer–promoter contacts, and decreases Pol II loading and productive elongation at the UBALD1 locus. The order is therefore: ZNF143 depletion → loss of DNA binding at the UBALD1 regulatory element → reduced coactivator/Pol II recruitment and looping → lower UBALD1 mRNA. Hence UBALD1 expression is expected to fall relative to the matched unperturbed control, with the effect emerging over the hours-to-days timescale typical of transcriptional responses.

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific activator: it binds the SPH/SBS motif (a CGCCTC-like element) through its zinc-finger DNA-binding domain and, once tethered, recruits co-activators to drive transcription of its targets — so the regulatory relationship recorded here is activating rather than repressive. If instead the assay were an acute depletion with a very short time course, the mRNA change would lag behind the loss of chromatin occupancy; but the eventual, matched-control comparison still reads as reduced expression, not increased.

POU5F1 (OCT4) acts as a transcriptional activator at the Utf1 locus: OCT4, together with SOX2, occupies the Utf1 promoter/enhancer and drives its transcription in pluripotent cells, making Utf1 a canonical core-pluripotency target. So when OCT4 protein is lost or reduced, the activating input at that regulatory region is removed first — occupancy at the Utf1 promoter drops, the enhancer/promoter is no longer trans-activated (and the surrounding pluripotency network, including SOX2 and NANOG, destabilizes as a downstream consequence), and Utf1 mRNA is no longer produced at its normal rate. The order is therefore: OCT4 protein loss → loss of activating occupancy/transactivation at the Utf1 regulatory region → decline in Utf1 transcript. Utf1 expression goes down relative to the matched unperturbed control.

PTPRK is a canonical TGF-β/SMAD3 transcriptional target, and in this setting NOTCH1 acts as a co-activator of that axis rather than its brake. On ligand engagement, NOTCH1 is cleaved to release the intracellular domain (NICD1), which binds SMAD3 directly and is recruited with RBP-Jκ/CSL to the PTPRK promoter, where the NICD1–SMAD3 complex (together with Notch-driven TGF-β1 autocrine signaling) boosts SMAD3-dependent transcription. Reducing NOTCH1 therefore removes this co-activating input: there is less nuclear NICD1 to partner with SMAD3 at the promoter, and less amplification of TGF-β/SMAD3 signaling, so SMAD3 occupancy and transactivation at PTPRK fall. Order of events: NOTCH1 loss → reduced NICD1 → diminished NICD1–SMAD3 cooperation (and reduced TGF-β1 autocrine support) → weaker SMAD3-driven PTPRK transcription → lower PTPRK mRNA/protein relative to the matched unperturbed control.

Under hypoxia, HIF1A transactivates the miR-210 locus (the canonical "hypoxamiR"), so a gain-of-activation of miR-210 mimics the HIF1A-driven arm of the hypoxic response. miR-210 is a direct repressor of E2F3: its seed sequence pairs with complementary sites in the E2F3 3′ UTR, recruiting the RISC/Argonaute complex to cleave and translationally block the transcript. The causal order is therefore HIF1A → miR-210 induction → miR-210:E2F3 3′ UTR binding → reduced E2F3 mRNA stability and translation → lower E2F3 protein. Net effect is downward, since E2F3 is a downstream target of the microRNA rather than an upstream activator of it. Functionally this fits the hypoxia program: dampening E2F3 restrains E2F-driven G1/S progression, helping cells slow proliferation while they adapt metabolically.

FOXK1 reduction is expected to lower ANKRD27 because FOXK1 acts as a chromatin-level cofactor for the ANKRD27 regulator TP63 rather than by changing TP63 abundance: FOXK1 occupies the enhancer anchors of p63-dependent regulatory loops, and it is what keeps those p63-bound enhancers physically connected to target promoters. When FOXK1 is depleted, the enhancer–promoter contacts that deliver p63 to the ANKRD27 locus are weakened/uncoupled, so TP63-dependent transcription of ANKRD27 drops. Order of events: FOXK1 loss → destabilized p63-dependent enhancer–promoter looping at the ANKRD27 locus → diminished TP63 transactivation → reduced ANKRD27 mRNA. Caveat: this holds where FOXK1 is actually engaged in the p63 program (neoplastic/squamous contexts with detectable FOXK1); where FOXK1 is not part of the p63 complex, the effect should be minimal and ANKRD27 would stay near control.

FOXK1 is not a regulator of TIMM50's own transcription factor but rather a physical co-factor of it: in squamous carcinoma cells TP63 (ΔNp63α) binds SCC-specific enhancers, and FOXK1 is recruited as the tumor-selective partner that forms the intermediate anchors holding those p63-bound enhancers in contact with distal target promoters. Loss of FOXK1 does not lower p63 protein, but it selectively weakens those p63-dependent enhancer–promoter loops, so the enhancer cannot deliver its activating input to the TIMM50 promoter. The causal order is therefore FOXK1 loss → collapse of the p63-dependent chromatin loop at the TIMM50 locus → reduced p63-driven enhancer activation → decreased TIMM50 transcription. Because the loop, not p63 abundance, is the limiting element, the effect is a decrease rather than an increase; the same phenotype is seen with p63 knockdown, and FOXK1 knockout phenocopies p63 loss for this class of targets.

Because REST represses L1CAM by binding the RE1/NRSE silencer and then recruiting CoREST and the BRG1-containing SWI/SNF (BAF) complex, whose ATP-dependent nucleosome remodeling and associated HDAC/H3K9-methyltransferase activity are what actually establish the closed, silenced promoter. BRG1/SMARCA4 loss therefore does not remove REST from the DNA so much as strip the repression complex of the remodeler it depends on: REST–CoREST can still be recruited, but the promoter fails to be compacted and de-acetylated, the repressive chromatin mark is not maintained, and L1CAM is de-repressed. The order is BRG1 loss → defective REST–CoREST–SWI/SNF repressor assembly/remodeling → loss of silencing at the L1CAM RE1 element → increased L1CAM transcription, i.e., L1CAM goes up relative to the matched unperturbed control.

KMT2D is the catalytic subunit of the KMT2D–COMPASS-like complex, the H3K4 mono-methyltransferase that primes and maintains active enhancers by depositing H3K4me1 and, together with CBP/p300, promoting H3K27ac. In erythroid precursors GATA1 binds distal enhancers and, on a subset of them, recruits this complex; EPOR sits among the canonical GATA1-dependent erythroid genes whose regulatory elements are co-occupied by GATA1 and KMT2D. Order of events: loss of KMT2D → the COMPASS complex can no longer methylate H3K4 on those GATA1-bound enhancers → H3K4me1 and H3K27ac marks fall and the enhancers lose accessibility/activity → GATA1 occupancy and enhancer–promoter activation at the EPOR locus weaken → EPOR transcription declines. Because KMT2D acts as an obligate coactivator rather than a repressor of this axis, removing it removes the positive input, so EPOR expression is expected to go down relative to the matched unperturbed control.

Mechanism: miR-181b-1 is a STAT3-transcribed microRNA that directly base-pairs with the CYLD 3′UTR and represses it post-transcriptionally (argonaute-mediated mRNA destabilization/translational block). Order of events: STAT3 (activated downstream of IL-6/JAK) drives miR-181b-1 transcription → mature miR-181b-1 loads into RISC and silences CYLD mRNA → CYLD protein falls, relieving its deubiquitinase-mediated restraint on NF-κB. Perturbing the microRNA by loss/reduction removes that repressive arm, so CYLD mRNA/protein is de-repressed and rises — CYLD goes up relative to the matched unperturbed control. Key mediator = miR-181b-1 itself acting on CYLD; the downstream consequence is reduced NF-κB/IκB-kinase signaling and, in the reciprocal loop, dampened p-STAT3, since CYLD loss normally feeds forward to sustain STAT3 activation. The STAT3→CYLD relationship noted in the annotation is therefore indirect: STAT3 sets the level of the miR-181b-1 repressor rather than driving CYLD expression; the acute, dominant effect of miR-181b-1 knockdown is de-repression, i.e., CYLD up.

down

JUN (c-Jun/AP-1) acts upstream and positively on ETV4/PEA3-family transcription — the ETV4 promoter carries AP-1 elements, c-Jun transactivates it, and PEA3 factors cooperate with c-Jun/c-Fos at composite ETS/AP-1 enhancers. ETV4 in turn is a direct activator of NOTCH4: it binds the NOTCH4 promoter and drives its transcription (ChIP, siRNA knockdown, luciferase reporter and qPCR; PMID 21679465), so NOTCH4 transcript tracks ETV4 levels. With JUN reduced, ETV4 expression/activity drops first, ETV4 occupancy at the NOTCH4 promoter falls second, and NOTCH4 transcription decreases last — giving lower NOTCH4 than the matched unperturbed control in the same context. This assumes the modeled JUN→ETV4 edge is activating, as annotated for the AP-1/PEA3 axis; compensation by other AP-1 components would only dampen the magnitude.
